key_idea: Count per directed edge (D,B): (deg B - 1) * C(deg D - 1, 3) choices of A and {C,E,F}, minus the cases where A coincides with one of C,E,F, which is (triangles through edge DB) * C(deg D - 2, 2).
sketch: A sword is determined by its hub D, the neighbour B, the tip A in N(B)\{D} and an unordered triple from N(D)\{B}; the only invalid configurations are those where A is itself in the triple, which requires A to be a common neighbour of B and D. So compute the number of triangles through every edge with the standard degree-ordered orientation (each vertex keeps only edges to higher (degree,id) vertices, mark out-neighbours and scan) in O(m sqrt m), then sum the formula over both directions of every edge. Totals can approach 2e18, so I accumulate in unsigned __int128 and print manually. Pitfalls: C,E,F are unordered (edge sets define distinctness), and degree-1 offsets in the binomials. Verified against an O(sum deg^2) brute force on random small graphs.
